TIP 1: Senior partner blocked associate from leaving meeting
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 21 April 2026

I am an analyst at North Reach Capital. I was in Conference Room 18B on 14 April 2026 when Senior Partner Ben Coltrane berated associate Tessa Aleshire during the 4:00 PM portfolio review.

The argument started after Aleshire questioned the valuation assumptions for the Varro Health follow-on investment. Coltrane raised his voice, told her she was "too junior to grandstand," and stood between her and the door when she tried to leave. I saw him put his hand on the door frame and tell her the meeting was not over.

The people in the room were Coltrane, Aleshire, me, Principal Amara Cho, and associate Devin Lale. Aleshire began recording only after Coltrane blocked the door. I reported this to HR case NRC-2026-0417 on 17 April and have my notes from the meeting.

The meeting had already been tense because Aleshire's valuation memo challenged the revenue multiple used in the investment committee deck. Coltrane said she was "trying to embarrass the deal team" and asked who had encouraged her to bring it up. When she stood up, her notebook was closed and her laptop was already in her bag. That is why I believed she was trying to leave, not stage a confrontation.

After the incident, Cho told both associates to write down what they remembered before speaking with HR. I did that the same evening and emailed the notes to myself from my personal account. I am submitting this because the internal rumor has shifted toward blaming Aleshire, and that is not what I saw from my seat near the screen.

TIP 2: Associate staged confrontation with North Reach partner
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 22 April 2026

I was present for the 14 April 2026 portfolio review at North Reach Capital, and I believe the account circulating internally omits important context. Tessa Aleshire came into the meeting prepared to provoke Ben Coltrane about the Varro Health valuation.

Aleshire interrupted twice, had her phone already angled toward the table, and said she wanted a record for HR before Coltrane had raised his voice. Coltrane did stand near the door, but in my view he was trying to keep the meeting from spilling into the hallway while people from the investor-relations team were outside.

The room included Coltrane, Aleshire, Amara Cho, Devin Lale, and one analyst whose name I will not write here. I am not defending Coltrane's tone. I am saying Aleshire was recording before the alleged blocking happened, and the sequence matters.

There had been tension between Aleshire and the Varro deal team for weeks. On 11 April she told me she was tired of being ignored and that "HR listens when there is a record." During the meeting, she placed her phone screen-down near her notebook before the valuation discussion started. When Coltrane challenged her assumptions, she touched the phone and said, "Please repeat that."

I agree Coltrane should not have raised his voice. I also think the current version being circulated leaves out Aleshire's preparation and makes it sound like she only recorded for safety after being blocked. My concern is that HR will treat every witness who mentions this context as protecting a senior partner. I am trying to preserve the sequence accurately.

TIP 3: HR asked witnesses to keep North Reach incident informal
CHANNEL: intake form
RECEIVED: 23 April 2026

I work in operations at North Reach Capital. I was not in Conference Room 18B during the 14 April 2026 meeting, but I helped collect witness calendars after HR opened case NRC-2026-0417.

The same incident is being described in opposite ways. One witness statement says Ben Coltrane blocked Tessa Aleshire from leaving after the Varro Health discussion. Another says Aleshire began recording before Coltrane moved near the door and was trying to bait him into an HR complaint.

HR business partner Livia Morn asked me on 18 April to keep the matter "informal until partnership decides posture." I have the calendar export, the witness list, and Morn's Teams message. I am submitting this because the firm may bury the competing accounts instead of preserving them.

The witness list itself shows why the accounts should be preserved carefully. Amara Cho's statement describes Coltrane standing by the door after Aleshire got up. Devin Lale's draft statement, which I saw in the HR folder, says Aleshire was recording before Coltrane moved. The analyst's calendar note says only "Varro review escalated," which does not resolve the sequence.

I am not taking a side on who was right in the investment debate. My concern is process. The firm has a financial reason to keep Coltrane stable on the Varro follow-on, and it also has a reputational reason not to appear to punish an associate who raised valuation concerns. That combination makes an informal handling especially risky.
